clips.text: "Enjoy" emphasizes the pleasure you get from an activity. When another verb follows it, use "-ing": "I enjoy reading." Do not say "I enjoy to read."
"Goodbye" is formal, and "bye" is short and casual. Use "see you later" or "see you tomorrow" when you expect to see the person again.
"Hello" is neutral, "hi" is more casual, and "good morning", "good afternoon", and "good evening" depend on the time of day.
"I like reading" often focuses on enjoying the activity. "I like to read before class" can focus on a preference or habit. This is a difference in focus, not a strict rule.
"I like to read" does not mean "I want to read." The first describes a liking. The second describes a wish.
"I want to finish high school" can also describe a goal in context. "My goal is to finish high school" names it directly. The meaning also depends on the context.
"I want to study next year" expresses a wish with a time. It does not prove that a plan is ready. Use "I plan to study next year" when you want to state a plan.
"I would like to learn English" means I want to learn English, expressed more politely or softly. Use "would like to + base verb," not "would like + verb-ing" for this meaning.
A basic sentence in English usually needs a subject and a verb. Start with this pattern: “Subject + Verb + Complement.”
A full sentence needs more than "to read" or "reading." Use a subject and a main verb: "I like reading." "I want to read."
A letter has a name, but it can have different sounds in words.
A personal introduction tells people who you are, what you do, what you like, and what you want for your future. Choose words that match your own ideas.
A singular noun refers to one person, animal, place, or thing. A plural noun normally refers to two or more.

Use "but" for a contrast: "I like to study alone, but I enjoy working with my classmates."
Use "like + noun" to name something you like: "I like music." "I like books."
Use "like + verb-ing" for an activity you like: "I like reading." "I like playing soccer."
Use "plan to + base verb" to say what you intend to do: "I plan to take an English course next year." A plan is not a promise that the action will happen.
Use "someday" for an unspecified future time, "next year" for the following year, and "this year" for the current year. "I would like to travel someday." "I plan to study English this year."
Use "want to + base verb" for something you want to do: "I want to learn English." Wanting something does not show that you already have a plan.
Use subject + am/is/are + information: "I am a student." "She is a nurse." "They are students."

Use “I” for the person who speaks and “you” for the person who listens. Use “he” for a man or boy, “she” for a woman or girl, and “it” for a thing, place, idea, or animal. For a pet you know, you can use “he” or “she.”
Use “a” before a consonant sound and “an” before a vowel sound: “a teacher,” “a university student,” “an engineer,” “an assistant.”
Use “a” or “an” with one countable singular noun: “a brother,” “an activity.” Do not use “a” or “an” before a plural noun: “two brothers,” “many activities.”

Use “we” for the speaker and one or more people. “You” can mean one person or several people. Use “they” for two or more people, animals, things, or ideas. You can also use “they” for one person when you do not know the person's gender or when the person uses “they.”
